snippet.title: A Radio Signal with an Unexpected Listener
snippet.description:
In 1980s Brazil, Clip Informática on Radio USP in São Paulo sent computer programs over the air as sound. A listener could record the signal onto cassette; a compatible home computer could then try to read its patterns as data. The path ran from station to radio, cassette, and computer—but distortion, recording level, playback speed, and compatibility all mattered.

Datassette catalogues its copy of episode 102 with a 1987 date and MSX software audio near the end. Separately, developer Weber Kai identified an online recording as episode 102 and described trying to decode it.

Kai reported a match with the MSX game Avenger. We haven’t independently repeated his decoding, established that the two recordings are identical, or verified a game launch. His public notes do not provide a complete comparison record.

snippet.title: She Saved 13 Kids in a Blizzard #BlizzardOf1888 #Shorts
snippet.description:
When a Nebraska school began coming apart in the 1888 blizzard, Minnie Freeman tied thirteen pupils together with twine she had taken from a boy who was playing with it in class.

Carrying the youngest, she led the children through the storm toward a farmhouse three-quarters of a mile away. All thirteen made it to safety.

snippet.title: Why Is This Cat on a Monument? #history #shorts
snippet.description:
Why is a cat featured on a monument to a scholar who helped unlock the Maya script? Yuri Knorozov’s Siamese companion, Asya, came into his life years after his breakthrough. A former student recalled that he even tried to credit her as a co-author of research on signaling—and the monument recreates a famous photograph of the two together.

snippet.title: A Diver Reached for a Hand in a Sunken Tugboat. It Grabbed Back. #HarrisonOkene #Jascon4
snippet.description:
Harrison Okene was the cook aboard the tugboat Jascon-4 when it sank off the coast of Nigeria on 26 May 2013, at a depth of about 30 metres. Trapped inside the wreck, he survived for more than 60 hours in an air pocket.

A diver sent to recover bodies reached for a hand — and it grabbed back. Okene was the only survivor among the 12 people aboard; the other 11 crew members died. Divers brought him to the surface in a diving bell before transferring him to a decompression chamber.

snippet.title: We Found Their Tools. Where Are Their Clothes?
snippet.description:
Stone tools survived for more than a million years. Almost all the clothes disappeared.

Follow a tiny ancient sandal into a journey through Western European clothing: Roman tunics, medieval layers, Amsterdam in 1559, extravagant court outfits, enormous crinolines, and the strikingly different dresses of the 1920s.

One riverbank connects the eras in a richly detailed paper-diorama world. And at the end, the question turns toward us: what will people make of the clothes we leave behind?

Which outfit would you wear today?

Historical scenes are illustrative recreations. The future museum is imagined.
